questions.q: Per this lesson, how do the SOQL query and CPU time governor limits differ between synchronous and asynchronous Apex?
options: Synchronous Apex gets 100 SOQL queries and 10,000 ms CPU time per transaction; asynchronous Apex gets 200 SOQL queries and 60,000 ms CPU time
Synchronous and asynchronous Apex share identical limits for both SOQL queries and CPU time
Synchronous Apex gets more SOQL queries and more CPU time than asynchronous Apex
Asynchronous Apex has no governor limits at all
questions.explain: Asynchronous Apex gets meaningfully higher limits on both counts precisely because it isn't blocking a real-time interaction -- which is exactly why heavy or bulk logic gets pushed to async in the first place.

questions.q: What does this lesson say an architect gives up by moving work from synchronous to asynchronous execution?
options: Nothing -- asynchronous execution is strictly better with no downside
Certainty about when the work actually happens, and the tight, immediate feedback loop to the user -- an async failure doesn't automatically surface back to the original transaction
The ability to use SOQL queries at all
Access to custom objects and fields
questions.explain: Because the async job is decoupled from the triggering transaction, the user who already moved on isn't automatically told if it later fails -- that notification has to be deliberately designed, since the platform doesn't surface it the way a synchronous exception would.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which scenario is a strong candidate for synchronous execution rather than asynchronous?
options: A nightly rollup calculation that doesn't need to finish immediately
A bulk update touching tens of thousands of records
A screen that displays a calculated result or blocks a save, where the next UI state depends on the outcome before the user moves on
A non-urgent integration sync that can run whenever Salesforce schedules it
questions.explain: When the user needs to see the result before the next step can happen, async would mean showing an unready or missing result -- that's exactly the case for keeping the operation synchronous.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against treating 'move it to async' as an automatic fix for governor-limit pressure?
options: Because asynchronous Apex is always slower than synchronous Apex in practice
Because asynchronous Apex cannot be used with Batch or Scheduled Apex
Because Salesforce charges extra for asynchronous Apex execution
Because it skips weighing the loss of the immediate feedback loop and the need to explicitly design how an async failure gets noticed and handled
questions.explain: The senior version of this decision asks what the user or process actually needs from the timing of the result, not just whether current limits are tight -- jumping straight to async without that analysis, and without a failure-notification plan, is the junior mistake this lesson calls out.

questions.q: What specific design question must an architect answer whenever they choose to move a piece of logic to asynchronous Apex?
options: Who notices and handles an async failure -- for example through a retry mechanism, an error log an admin reviews, or an alert on job failure
Whether the org has purchased enough Salesforce licenses
Whether the Lightning Experience theme supports asynchronous components
Whether the object involved has at least one custom field
questions.explain: Because the default platform behavior doesn't automatically tell anyone that an async job failed, the architect must deliberately build a way for a failure to be noticed and acted on -- this is the explicit cost the lesson says comes with choosing async.
